title: Examining the Usage of Generative AI Models in Student Learning Activities for Software Programming
extended_summary:
This paper examines how access to generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, affects student learning in programming tasks, with a focus on both task performance and knowledge gains. The authors argue that prior work has largely emphasized whether AI can solve educational tasks or improve performance, while paying less attention to whether students actually learn the underlying concepts. Their research questions address students’ perceptions of ChatGPT, its effect on programming task performance, its effect on conceptual understanding, and the ways students interact with the tool across different proficiency levels.

The study used a controlled 2×2 between-subjects experiment comparing beginner versus intermediate undergraduate programmers, and ChatGPT access versus no-ChatGPT access. Twenty-four undergraduates from a Canadian university were recruited from introductory and intermediate programming courses and assigned into four groups of six. All participants watched a 10-minute instructional video on the Dynamic Sliding Window technique, then completed a 30-minute LeetCode-style programming task. Students in the treatment condition could use GPT-3.5-turbo only, while the comparison group could use conventional online resources such as documentation and Stack Overflow but not AI tools. The researchers collected code submissions, generated test-case performance results, survey responses, open-ended explanations of solutions and concepts, chat histories, and screen recordings.

The main findings show that ChatGPT substantially improved task performance for beginners, especially when they used it to generate complete solutions, but this did not consistently translate into stronger conceptual understanding. Intermediate students performed similarly with or without ChatGPT on the coding task, but those without ChatGPT generally demonstrated stronger understanding of both their solutions and the underlying concept. The qualitative analysis also showed that beginners tended to rely more heavily on complete-solution generation, whereas intermediates were more likely to use stepwise prompting. The authors conclude that generative AI can support task completion, but without guidance it may encourage over-reliance and weaker learning. They recommend that educators and students use GenAI as a structured learning aid rather than primarily as a problem-solving shortcut.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model used for question answering, code generation, explanation, and programming assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Undergraduate beginners and intermediate programming students used ChatGPT (specifically GPT-3.5-turbo, normalized to ChatGPT) as the only external aid while solving a programming task on the dynamic sliding window technique; the study compared ChatGPT-assisted participants with peers using conventional online resources.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT access improved programming task performance for beginners. Beginner participants with ChatGPT passed an average of 410.7 tests versus 80.7 for beginners without ChatGPT, and this difference was reported as statistically significant (p = 0.015).
findings.measure: Programming task performance measured as number of passed test cases out of 500 on a coding task

findings.finding_summary: For intermediate students, ChatGPT did not improve task performance relative to conventional resources. Intermediate participants with ChatGPT averaged 291.0 passed tests, compared with 290.8 for intermediates without ChatGPT.
findings.measure: Programming task performance measured as number of passed test cases out of 500 on a coding task

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-supported complete solution generation substantially increased task success but was not associated with stronger knowledge gains. Participants using Complete Solution Generation averaged 495 passed tests versus 206.7 for Stepwise Code Generation, a statistically significant difference (p = 0.032), yet only one of the 12 ChatGPT users who were analyzed for interaction strategy demonstrated strong understanding.
findings.measure: Programming task performance and coded knowledge-gain categories from post-study explanations

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT use was associated with weaker solution understanding than conventional resources. Among beginners with ChatGPT, 4/6 showed weak solution understanding, while beginners without ChatGPT had only 1/6 rated weak; among intermediates with ChatGPT, 3/6 were partial and 3/6 weak, whereas intermediates without ChatGPT had 4/6 strong and 2/6 partial understanding.
findings.measure: Coded solution-understanding levels from open-ended post-study responses

findings.finding_summary: For conceptual understanding, ChatGPT showed different patterns by proficiency. Intermediate students without ChatGPT showed stronger concept understanding (3/6 strong, 3/6 partial) than intermediates with ChatGPT (3/6 partial, 3/6 weak), while beginners with ChatGPT showed a slightly better distribution (1/6 strong, 2/6 partial, 3/6 weak) than beginners without ChatGPT (5/6 partial, 1/6 weak).
findings.measure: Coded concept-understanding levels from open-ended post-study responses

quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled between-subjects experiment with a comparison condition and randomized blocks across proficiency and ChatGPT access, but the sample is small (n=24) and outcomes include researcher-coded understanding measures rather than standardized assessments.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear positive effects on task completion for beginners, but impacts on learning/knowledge gains are mixed or negative and no standardized effect sizes are reported, so overall educational impact is unclear.
